summary:
Jezero Marswalk Navigator is a web-based map that helps astronauts plan and carry out a surface excursion in Jezero Crater. Built on NASA’s CTX orbital mosaic from JPL Mars Trek, it lets a crew choose walking or rover travel, pick a mission goal, and get a route with named start and end points, the stops in between, and the purpose of each. An astronaut or rover icon moves along the route like a GPS, and the route recalculates from any new position. The tool tracks Martian time of day and checks that the crew can return before sunset. At the end of a rover trip, it asks again whether the crew is walking or driving back, in case the rover runs out of fuel.
For each stop, the app shows terrain roughness measured from the imagery, temperature, wind and pressure from Perseverance’s MEDA, radiation from Curiosity’s RAD, storm and solar-alert scenarios, geology, and real Perseverance photos.
It addresses the challenge by combining several NASA datasets into one hyperlocal view for a Marswalk. This matters because safe, well-informed exploration will be essential for the first human missions to Mars.
details:
Jezero Marswalk Navigator is an interactive survival guide for travelling across Jezero Crater on Mars, the site where NASA’s Perseverance rover is searching for signs of ancient life. The user chooses how they travel (on foot or by rover), picks a destination, and sets a departure time in local Mars time. They also choose conditions: clear sky, dust storm, or dust storm with a solar particle alert. The app plots the route on a real NASA map and lists every stop with distance, travel time and the reason to go there. A live GPS simulation then walks the traveller along the route, with Mars time, remaining daylight, a return-by deadline and rover fuel all tracked. The user can also simulate a fuel failure to see how the plan changes.

Toggleable map layers add optical, topographic, thermal, spectral, geophysical, atmospheric, radiation, chemical and hazard views. A catalogue of every Jezero landmark explains why it matters, including its geology, chemistry, hazards and travel time on foot or by rover.
Mars has dust storms, temperatures near -80°C, steep cliffs and craters, and no GPS or rescue. Our tool turns scattered science data into a clear, readable plan, so crews, students and mission planners can see which route is safest, how long it takes, and when to turn back.
We want to make Mars exploration easier to understand and plan, and to inspire people to see Jezero as a place they could explore. The same approach could support mission planning, education and public outreach, and later extend to other Martian sites.
The Data and tools used are NASA open data and imagery; the CTX mosaic (6 m per pixel) from NASA/JPL/USGS via Mars Trek, Perseverance raw images, and the USGS-NASA Planetary Geologic Mapping Program. Science references from Mars missions, MEDA (temperature and wind), MSL RAD (radiation), CRISM, HiRISE, RIMFAX, PIXL and SHERLOC. Built as a single self-contained web page with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The map is drawn in SVG, and the intro and simulation use the Web Animations API.
It is creative as the design and ideas and most of coding was done by us, the site opens with a cinematic zoom from the solar system down to Mars. The route is built from a graph of real landmarks, so it works like a travel guide rather than a plain map. The traveller can choose a walking or rover route, adjust the weather and see what happens if fuel fails.
We considered safety; return-by time, sunrise and sunset, dust, radiation and slope hazards. Landing site, Western Delta and Western Breach use NASA coordinates, while other stops are placed on the imagery. Walking pace, rover speed and fuel use are labelled as planning assumptions.
The site works in any browser with no install, and respects reduced-motion settings.
For future work we could see a 3D map enhancements, hill shading, customised mobility, long-term usability and polish.
